title: Clock and Lantern
premise: In the winter of 1863, during a grinding border war, battlefield nurse Wendell Eriksen keeps a private ledger of soldiers whose deaths officers have erased to protect reputations and promotions. When a stranger arrives bearing a letter in the handwriting of Captain Aldous Vey—a man officially dead for a year—Wendell realizes Vey is alive, hiding, and the ledger's most important name. Together they must smuggle the ledger and Vey's testimony past three military checkpoints to a tribunal that convenes in eleven days. Betrayal at the second checkpoint forces Wendell to choose between the law that would hang Vey as a deserter and the justice the ledger demands; in the end, Wendell testifies under a false name, the corrupt general falls, and Vey surrenders himself—while Wendell, identity deliberately blurred, walks away to start a new ledger in a new town.
about_author: Ivo Sandoval is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military hospital records before turning to fiction. They write historical fiction about the people official histories leave out, and live quietly near a river with too many books.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. At the field hospital at Marrow Creek, Wendell tends the wounded by day and records erased names by night—men reported as deserters, suicides, or simply struck from rolls. A colonel visits, asking odd questions about paperwork. Emotional beat: quiet dread; Wendell understands the ledger has grown dangerous.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Lantern
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. On a freezing night a gaunt stranger, calling himself Tomas Rill, arrives seeking treatment and recognizes Wendell's careful hand on a supply form. He waits, watches, and says nothing—yet. Emotional beat: wary curiosity; Wendell notices the stranger's officer's posture beneath the rags.

chapters.title: Handwriting of a Dead Man
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Rill reveals himself as Captain Aldous Vey, officially dead since the disaster at Harrow Ford, and produces a letter in his own hand that the army used to posthumously blame him for the rout. He asks Wendell to help prove who really gave the fatal order. Emotional beat: shock hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Names That Cost Money
chapters.summary: POV Vey. Vey explains the machinery: General Corvane sold the Harrow Ford positions and buried the evidence under dead men's names—names Wendell has been recording all along. Emotional beat: fury; Vey realizes Wendell's ledger may be the only surviving map of the crime.

chapters.title: Eleven Days to the Tribunal
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. A sympathetic clerk, Miss Ansel, confirms a civilian tribunal in the capital will hear corruption evidence—but only within eleven days, and only with corroborating documents. Wendell and Vey plan the route: three checkpoints along the river road. Emotional beat: the clock starts; fear becomes purpose.

chapters.title: What the Nurse Carries
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Wendell copies the ledger into cipher, hides the original, and says goodbye to the hospital that gave them cover and identity. A fellow nurse, Brann, grows suspicious. Emotional beat: grief for the self being left behind; identity begins to feel like a costume.

chapters.title: The River Road
chapters.summary: POV Vey. The two travel as a nurse and a wounded cousin. Vey, unused to being powerless, chafes while Wendell's competence carries them. First sight of the checkpoint at Toll Bridge. Emotional beat: grudging mutual respect forming under strain.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Toll Bridge
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. A young, frightened lieutenant searches their cart; Wendell bluffs with forged transfer papers and a genuine act of triage on a wounded guard, buying passage. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by guilt—Wendell has learned to weaponize care.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed the Order
chapters.summary: POV Vey. In a river town, Vey finds Major Quist, the officer who actually signed the Harrow Ford order, now a drunk hiding from Corvane. Quist agrees to testify—then disappears in the night, leaving a bloodied collar button. Emotional beat: hope raised and snatched away; the enemy is close.

chapters.title: Brann on the Road
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Brann catches up, not as a betrayer but as a deserter of her own—she recognized Corvane's name in Wendell's questions and has her own erased brother in the ledger. She joins them. Emotional beat: unexpected solidarity; the ledger's names have families.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Quarantine Camp
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. The camp at Fenlow requires papers and a surgeon's inspection. Wendell passes; Vey is recognized by an old sergeant who hesitates—then salutes and lets them through, choosing memory over orders. Emotional beat: the theme crystallized—justice living outside the law, in individuals.

chapters.title: What Corvane Buys
chapters.summary: POV Vey. A messenger offers Vey a pardon and a commission if he vanishes; Corvane knows they're coming. Vey refuses and sends the messenger back with a message of defiance. Emotional beat: temptation weighed and refused; the stakes turn personal and mortal.

chapters.title: The Trap at Fenlow
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. The sergeant's mercy was reported. Troopers sweep the camp; Brann is taken, and the cipher ledger copy is nearly seized before Wendell burns a decoy and hides the real pages in a coffin bound for the capital. Emotional beat: terror and sacrifice; the cost becomes real.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Lantern
chapters.summary: POV Brann. In a holding tent, Brann endures questioning and gives nothing—until she learns they mean to hang Vey on sight as a deserter rather than risk a trial. She escapes through the latrine trench. Emotional beat: endurance; justice and law visibly splitting apart.

chapters.title: The Coffin Ride
chapters.summary: POV Vey. The three regroup and Vey rides with the ledger inside a coffin in a funeral cortege, lying still among the actual dead of the war he's blamed for. Emotional beat: haunting meditation on identity—Vey among the erased, nearly one of them.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Capital Gate
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. The city gate is Corvane's last wall; the commandant has orders to detain 'a nurse with a box.' Wendell invokes a tribunal witness statute with a bluff built on Miss Ansel's paperwork, forcing the commandant to choose between Corvane and the law. Emotional beat: the law itself becomes the weapon—barely.

chapters.title: Miss Ansel's Betrayal
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. At the tribunal steps, Miss Ansel is waiting—with Corvane's men. She was turned months ago; the tribunal summons was the trap. Vey is arrested; Wendell escapes with the ledger only because Brann creates a diversion and is recaptured. Emotional beat: devastation; the plan was never theirs.

chapters.title: The Empty Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Hiding in the capital's archives, Wendell discovers the cipher copy Corvane seized is the decoy—the real pages remain sewn in the coffin lining. But a tribunal needs a witness, not just paper, and Wendell has no legal name that can't be erased. Emotional beat: the theme of identity at its sharpest; anonymity becomes armor.

chapters.title: Testimony of a Nobody
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Wendell walks into the tribunal as 'a nurse of no regiment' and, protected by a procedural loophole Ansel's own trap created, reads the ledger aloud—name after erased name—while the coffin is brought in as evidence. Emotional beat: the climax; quiet voice against institutional power, and the room turning.

chapters.title: Corvane's Fall
chapters.summary: POV Vey. Confronted with his own forged order and the ledger's corroborating supply records, Corvane unravels, attempting to shift blame until his own adjutant testifies against him. Vey, in chains, watches justice arrive from outside the law that condemned him. Emotional beat: catharsis without triumph.

chapters.title: Sentences
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Corvane is court-martialed; Vey's death sentence is commuted to a year's confinement for his desertion—the law exacting its small price even as it concedes the larger truth. Brann is freed; Miss Ansel, it emerges, turned only to save her own erased brother. Emotional beat: bittersweet accounting; no justice arrives clean.

chapters.title: A New Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Wendell visits Vey once behind bars, leaves him the original ledger to read, and walks out of the capital with a blank notebook and no name anyone can find. In a river town far away, Wendell opens the notebook to the first page. Emotional beat: resolution—identity chosen, justice carried forward by hand and lantern.
